primitives.name: Accelerometer-Based Sleep Detection
primitives.verbatim_quote: The system of claim 11 wherein the one or more sensors include an accelerometer configured to provide data to the processor for detecting the sleep state or the waking event.
primitives.assumptions: User motion is representative of sleep/wake cycles; accelerometer data is temporally synchronized.
primitives.breakdown_regime: High-frequency oscillations during wakefulness cause signal saturation or noise dominance.

layer2.mapping: Accelerometer-derived motion patterns map to Markovian state transitions in sleep-wake cycle classification.
layer2.telemetry: Motion magnitude variance over time windows

primitives.name: Galvanic Skin Response Monitoring
primitives.verbatim_quote: The system of claim 11 wherein the one or more sensors measure a galvanic skin response of the user.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'GSR(t)': 'galvanic skin response in Siemens', 't': 'time in seconds'}
primitives.assumptions: Skin conductance correlates with sympathetic nervous system activity; baseline drift is accounted for.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Low GSR values below threshold indicate stable physiological equilibrium.

layer2.mapping: GSR modulates arousal probability in latent variable models of autonomic regulation.

primitives.name: Heart Rate Windowed Quality Metric
primitives.verbatim_quote: The computer program product of claim 16 wherein the window of heart rate data includes a predetermined duration within the slow wave sleep period having a highest quality of heart rate data according to the data quality metric.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'HR(t)': 'heart rate in beats per minute', 'Q(t)': 'data quality index dimensionless', 't': 'time in seconds'}
primitives.assumptions: Slow wave sleep has minimal noise in HR; quality metric is defined by signal-to-noise ratio.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Signal artifacts during REM or movement invalidate quality thresholds.

layer2.mapping: Windowed HR quality maps to entropy-based uncertainty in cardiac dynamics during deep sleep.
layer2.telemetry: Entropy of HR variability within fixed time segments

Heart rate quality ensures reliable physiological metrics during slow-wave sleep. These are combined into a probabilistic model where each sensor contributes a likelihood factor. The system's failure mode occurs when sensor fusion lacks temporal alignment or when physiological noise exceeds signal fidelity. The derived kernel of GSR and HR quality supports a latent variable model of recovery, where arousal probability modulates sleep depth. The isomorphism between motion and state transition enables robust classification under noisy conditions. Dualities emerge in how motion and autonomic signals encode similar information—sleep state—through different modalities. The system's robustness depends on cross-validation of these modalities against known sleep stages.
